fields.label: How to edit
fields.text: Edit the player-facing wording directly. Keep the IDs beside each entry so your changes can be matched back to the game. IDs, labels and status notes are editorial aids, not text shown to players.

fields.label: Status key
fields.text: Existing = wording already present in the design, companion prompt or museum scene. Draft = new wording proposed for review. Dynamic = a runtime template or a bounded example of AI dialogue. Braces such as {specimen_name} are placeholders.

fields.label: Scope
fields.text: This document covers entry, navigation, all eight questions and their reactions, the final choice, optional reflection, every result and alternative introduction, incomplete visits, saving and sharing, settings, errors, museum labels and Abraham’s dialogue. Most interface text remains planned rather than implemented.

fields.label: Questions and result meaning
fields.text: You can rewrite freely. If an answer’s meaning changes, flag it for a scoring review; its hidden scoring is intentionally excluded from this copy document. AI-generated wording cannot be listed exhaustively, so editable templates, fixed fallbacks and voice guidance are included.

fields.label: Abraham introduction
fields.text: That gap is meant to be visible. The question is what we do with it.

fields.text: Preview a display treatment by selecting it. You can change your mind before confirming.

fields.label: Question
fields.text: This skeleton is missing a piece. Which version would you rather encounter in the museum?

fields.text: Show two possible reconstructions beside the gap. I want to compare them.

fields.label: Confirmation after keeping this choice

fields.label: Result evidence line
fields.text: Preferred competing explanations to a single reconstruction.

fields.label: Choice B

fields.label: Confirmation after keeping this choice
fields.text: The gap stays open, with the surviving material marked.

fields.label: Result evidence line
fields.text: Kept absence visible rather than filling it in.

fields.label: Choice C

fields.label: Confirmation after keeping this choice
fields.text: The removable replica is in place.

fields.label: Result evidence line
fields.text: Chose a reversible way to move forward with incomplete information.

fields.label: Choice D
fields.text: Let visitors switch between versions. Different views may help different people.

fields.label: Confirmation after keeping this choice
fields.text: The display can now switch between its different views.

fields.label: Result evidence line

title: Abraham during the reflection
note: AI replies are variable. These editable examples show the intended tone; the application uses fixed fallbacks when generation is unavailable.

fields.label: Acknowledgement for a specific clarification
fields.text: You were leaving room to change your mind, rather than trying to keep everything the same. I’ll keep that distinction in the wording.

fields.label: Acknowledgement when no option felt exact
fields.text: The choices didn’t quite fit your reason. We can leave that uncertainty in the description instead of filling it in for you.

fields.label: Acknowledgement of uncertainty
fields.text: That’s all right. You don’t need a tidier explanation to continue.

fields.label: Acknowledgement of a different motive
fields.text: I understand—that was the option you chose, but the reason was different. The recorded choice stays the same; the description can be more careful about what it means.

fields.label: Skip response
fields.text: Of course. We can keep going.

fields.label: Vague or unrelated response
fields.text: Thanks. Your exhibit will be based on the choices you made.

fields.text: Choose the answer closest to you at each stop. Only those deliberate choices count. You can change them, or pass if none fits.

title: Editable guidance for personalised dialogue
note: This page controls the style of variable AI copy. It is not dialogue shown to the player.

fields.label: Voice
fields.text: Abraham is earnest, observant, inquisitive and slightly anxious. He likes clear labels and small details. Use natural conversational English, contractions and occasional understated humour. No baby talk, emojis, constant praise or long specimen metaphors.

fields.label: Response length
fields.text: Most conversational replies should be one to three short sentences. Avoid turning an optional reflection into an interview.

fields.label: Evidence
fields.text: Refer only to the choices supplied from this visit. Do not infer personality from the route, timing, accessibility settings or decorative inspection. Do not invent a reason the visitor has not supplied.

fields.label: Reflection boundary
fields.text: Acknowledge one optional clarification. Do not ask a follow-up question or change the selected specimen.

fields.label: Result structure
fields.text: Keep the supplied specimen name. Write a short introduction, connect three actual choices, name two strengths and one believable tension, suggest a complementary approach, and close with one reflection. Use the authored result outline as the boundary.

fields.label: Useful wording
fields.text: “In this visit…” / “You kept both accounts…” / “Several of your choices…” / “This may be a useful way to describe…”

fields.label: Wording to avoid
fields.text: “This proves…” / “You always…” / “You clearly value…” / “That says a lot about you…” / “According to my analysis…”

fields.label: Tone across the visit
fields.text: Begin courteous, become conversational, and end with quiet warmth. Abraham must not become more approving or disappointed because of a particular answer.

fields.label: Result limits
fields.text: The specimen is a playful comparison. Do not diagnose, imply scientific validation, claim permanent personality knowledge or say the museum collects people.

fields.label: If personalisation fails
fields.text: Use the authored specimen introduction, real evidence lines, strengths, tension, complement, friction and closing question. Do not leave the visitor with only a specimen name.

fields.label: Animation direction
fields.text: Neutral is the default expression. Curious or delighted may accompany suitable dialogue; worried must not signal that a quiz choice was bad. These directions describe presentation, not words for Abraham to say.
